More or less on a question of privilege I should like to make a few remarks. I did not bring this matter up last night because it was getting close to eleven o'clock and I knew the minister was anxious to get the general item through. Can the minister give me an explanation of the anomalies that exist in the railway pass privileges for members of parliament? I understand that the passes of the members from Newfoundland are not affected, but on the other hand members coming, say, from Digby, Nova Scotia, to Saint John, New Brunswick, and from Vancouver to Victoria, or Victoria to Nanaimo, find their passes are not accepted on Canadian Pacific Railway steamships. I am wondering whether the minister himself,
Supply-Transport
when he visits our coast, which he unfortunately does not get an opportunity to do often enough, will get a pass on the Victoria-Nanaimo or Victoria-Vancouver boat. I am also informed that the -members of the legislature in Newfoundland have their own privileges. That may or may not be so. Is it true that they get pass privileges on the Canadian National steamship vessels operating to and from Newfoundland? If so, what part of the Railway Act entitles them to it? Are our passes valid on these lines under the same provision? If the minister cannot answer offhand, perhaps he will look into the matter -and see how it stands and what changes could possibly be made. Of course there is the question of subsidies involved. Some of the Canadian Pacific steamship lines get substantial subsidies from the government. If that is the basis upon which it is worked, I should like to have it looked into.

The only anomaly that I am aware
of is that concerning the movement outside of Canada, and it is on the line of the Canadian Pacific to the maritime provinces, part of which runs through the United States. The Railway Act clearly makes provision for free transportation to members of the House of Commons and of the other place in Canada.
I think that goes for the rest of the question that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni raised. The Railway Act gives no authority for free transportation on steamships.
Even if it is part of the transcontinental system?

Even if it is part of the
transcontinental system. That would exclude a car ferry, such as the Prince Edward Island car ferry, which -is considered a part of the railway system. If my hon. friend looks -at the pertinent section of the Railway Act he will see that the privileges of members in this regard are set out in detail. It certainly does not include transportation on the steamships.

On the other hand, one would think the steamship service from Digby, Nova Scotia, to Saint John, New Brunswick, would be included, because that is the only way in which the maritime members can get to their constituencies. I cannot swim to Vancouver, neither can the hon. member for Nanaimo. It must inevitably be part of our transcontinental system, and has always been -recognized as such. The mere fact that it is a wholly-owned subsidiary and called by -a different name should not obviate the responsibility of the

railway companies to recognize these passes. It is not a matter of great concern, but I am interested.

I can only be guided by what the act of parliament says. If the act were changed to meet that position, then of course the regulations would be put into effect to meet it; but as it is now, the position to which my hon. friend refers is not covered in the act.

Many amendments are introduced every year. I wonder whether that would not be an excellent amendment to bring down. We might open the Railway Act for one day and introduce the amendment. I am sure the minister will have to do it one of these days.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Cut out the steamship subsidies.
No; I think these are important. I have always believed that they were based on equity, and I am sure the minister would say that.

There is just one question I should like to ask. The matter has been brought up before. There are several members here from New Brunswick and several in the other place, who are obliged to go through the state of Maine in order to get to Ottawa. To do otherwise you would be obliged to go around to Moncton on the Canadian National Railway, and it would take an additional day to arrive in the capital city. These members are obliged to pay what is called a fee through Maine. It amounts today to around $10. The minister has said that it is a regulation. There is one thing that I fail to understand. I can send these receipts down to the Canadian Pacific Railway office here in Ottawa and within a few days I will get a cheque for the amount that I have paid. If I have two, three or four receipts they will give me a cheque for the full amount. It looks to me like a lot of bookkeeping for nothing. At one time I lost three or four receipts, and I know other hon. members have done the same thing. I do know of one member from New Brunswick who at one time had a through-Maine pass.
I would ask the minister to look into the matter to see if it is possible to have the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National issue passes to cover such travel. There are only about seven or eight members affected. It is a nuisance. There is no revenue involved so far as the railway is concerned, because the member is reimbursed when he sends the receipts to the Canadian Pacific Railway office.

I have given this matter careful consideration once before, and I have

come to the conclusion that unfortunately this cannot be done, because it is a part of a line over which neither parliament nor the board of transport commissioners have any jurisdiction. Parliament passed an act dealing with railways in Canada only. Similarly, the interstate commerce commission can confer no jurisdiction over United States lines in Canada, and unless there is a willingness on the part of the railways themselves to do it there is unfortunately nothing that can be done from this end.

Just one other question, Mr. Chairman. Is the cheque that is given to me by the Canadian Pacific Railway office a donation by the Canadian Pacific Railway, or a donation by the federal government; or where does it come from? I can send my receipts down and in a few days I get a cheque. It is a Canadian Pacific Railway cheque on the Bank of Montreal. Is it a contribution by the Canadian Pacific Railway to me as a member of parliament, or what is it?
I would think that it is.
Shame!
I presume the attitude they take is that since -under the terms of the act they cannot grant free transportation, they refund it in that manner.
Under what authority does the Canadian National Railways give Newfoundland members the privilege of riding free on their ships?
We do not get it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: And not the British Columbia members.

Because of the continuity of operation between Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, in the same manner as- there is -continuity of operation between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island so far as Prince Edward Idland is concerned.

There must be continuity of
operation between Saint John -and Digby, because, after all, the Dominion Atlantic Railway, which is a wholly owned subsidiary of the Canadian Pacific Railway, meets the train there.
No; the position is different, because one is a car ferry operated by the government through the Canadian National Railways, and the other service is operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.

Mr. Chairman, I
could never understand why it was considered necessary to grant these extraordinary privileges. I sympathize with hon. members who come from remote parts of the

country to help us run the affairs of the country, but frankly I am of the opinion that the time has long since passed when his extraordinary right to travel on passes should have been done away with. The other day, for instance, there was reference to hon. members of this house travelling free to Churchill. Travel free, by all means, but let us have vouchers filed with those charged with administration of these matters, so that they may have entries in their bookkeeping system in respect of each and every one of us who exercises this particular privilege. Honour those vouchers by all means; but let us not in this institution, where we enjoy such great privileges and where we are permitted to spend so freely-and not always our own money-let us not spend too freely the money which comes from our taxpayers. Let those vouchers be scrutinized in such a way that those who send us here will feel satisfied that they are receiving true value for the amounts covered by the vouchers passed by those in authority.
Ten years ago I travelled in my hon. friend's part of the country on a train on which only one passenger had paid his fare: all the rest of us were on some sort of free ticket, some sort of pass.

The Thursday train to
Toronto?

We carry these
tickets in our pocketbooks. I felt ashamed to travel on a pass on that train, because my business at that time was not political. I was not on that particular day saving the nation; rather I was transacting personal business ini my hon. friend's part of the world. I like him; he is a very fine gentleman, and I feel proud to be associated with him. But at that time I felt, as indeed I have felt for a decade since, that there was some doubt whether I should be travelling free on one of Canada's trains to do my own business.
It does not bother the hon. member on week ends?

I see over there one of the members from Vancouver, and I can say that I did the same thing in his part of the country, and felt equally ashamed.
The whole procedure of issuing free passes on a transportation system, whether it be rail to the Pacific coast, or the short-cut from Saint John to Digby, is questionable. One pays a few dollars extra to travel by that short-cut so as to save time. The procedure of issuing passes is something that should be looked into. We should try to find some method by which we can pay our own way to a greater extent, and not take so much for 80709-1274

granted or accept so readily the free transportation made available to us by the Railway Act. By the provisions of that act we are permitted to travel hither and yon, often for purposes of statesmanship, but oftener for personal business reasons. We are altogether too free in this practice. I see that the minister is busy consulting his deputies; perhaps it is about something more important than I am saying.
I repeat that the time is ripe for cutting down the number of free rides on the merry-go-round, even though we do get a brass ring. It is not too late to cut down this privilege of free transportation afforded to many of our citizens who, while they are not permitted to ride free on busses or aircraft-and I express the hope that the privilege may not be extended to those means of transportation-do travel free on trains and steamships.
When I say this my remarks are not directed to our tenth province of Newfoundland. I realize they must travel back and forth, and I hope that anything I say will not in any way limit their ingress or egress. I realize that our tenth province is a long distance away. Yet when I sit in a train and see the widows of Brown, Smith and Jones who have free transportation I feel that the time has come when a few dollars should be spent to investigate this high privilege which is given to many people. Most of them deserve it, but about ten per cent of them do not. It is a privilege which we as members of parliament, as well as our wives, sons and daughters, grandsons and granddaughters and sweethearts, enjoy when travelling on trains and steamships, and it is a privilege which should be checked and wherever possible curtailed. It should not be abused.
I have seen the privilege abused for over thirty years-and I shall not go into detail in the matter, although I could if I were asked to.
Would the hon. member be in favour of the cancellation of transportation privileges, so that only our expenses would be paid?

Yes, and that
vouchees should be supplied.

Then I have some observations to make on item 473. I should like to ask the minister a series of questions with regard to some of the canals in Ontario. Has the minister figures of the cost of maintaining and operating the Rideau canal? Are records kept of the number of boats of all descriptions passing through the canal, and if so, how many passed through in 1950 and in 1949?
The cost for the maintenance of the Rideau canal in these estimates is $368,565. We have a record of the number of boats passing through the canal, and I can get it for my hon. friend.
My next question concerns the Welland canal, in which I am more or less interested. Can the minister give the revenue derived from the operation of that canal in 1950?
I am afraid I shall have to get the figures for the hon. member.
From what sources is that revenue obtained?
It is mostly from the lease of lands and from the power development on the Welland canal.

In the public accounts of last year, $10,000 was provided for the transfer of lands and responsibilities in connection with the Welland feeder canal, and I understand that that amount was not used. Is there provision for a similar amount in the estimates this year?
The $10,000 was not used because an agreement was not effected between the township concerned and the department. It will be used this year if an agreement is completed.

What was the total
revenue from all canals in Canada in 1950?
$1,100,000 and some odd.

This item has to do with the St. Lawrence ship canal. Will the minister indicate what effect it is expected the construction of this canal will have upon the transportation system of Canada? Yesterday representations were made by the legislative committee of the railway brotherhoods in connection with this proposed St. Lawrence seaway, and they used these words:
We regard the value of the proposed seaway to Canada as theoretical, its cost very real, its need
[The Chairman.]
very doubtful, and its possible effect must be viewed with concern in so far as transportation is involved.
As the minister knows, last evening I suggested that there should be a commission or other body set up to study this whole question of the effect of the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway upon the transportation system of Canada. It might be possible to set up a committee of this house to consider the question. So far as we know, little thought has been given to the subject; yet it would appear to be of the utmost importance, particularly in view of the fact that with this Turgeon report we are entering upon a new day in transportation. This would seem to be the time to consider the whole transportation picture, of which the St. Lawrence seaway will be a most important part. Can the minister give us a review of the effects upon our transportation system that are expected to follow when the St. Lawrence seaway is built?

The railway brotherhoods have always opposed the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway, and in their briefs to the government they have set down reasons why it should not be proceeded with. Unfortunately, because of the estimates that concerned the Department of Transport, I was not present yesterday when they made their presentation to the government. But I have read the brief, and it is not at all dissimilar to those which have been presented on previous occasions.
The railways in the United States have carried on quite a militant opposition to the project. At one time the opposition in Canada was perhaps not unlike that in the United States, but I believe it has changed substantially. Notwithstanding the representations made by the brotherhoods, the former president of the Canadian National Railways declared himself to be in favour of the project for a number of reasons, the main one being that the industrial development which would arise would mean far more in the way of traffic to the railways than any loss that might occur.
My hon. friend speaks of the cost, and asks what studies have been made as to the benefits likely to be derived.
This is all quite interesting, but I did not mention the cost.
That was in the brief.

I referred not only to the benefits. What I had in mind was to get the general picture of the effect of the seaway upon our transportation system. I am not taking one side or the other; I simply want to get from the minister an indication of the general effect

upon our transportation system of the construction of the seaway.

I was trying to get to that, perhaps not in a manner which was entirely suitable to my hon. friend. What I intended to say was that, on the economic side, studies were made over a considerable length of time by various groups in the country. These studies were made by boards of engineers, both United States and Canadian; by engineers from Ontario and Quebec, and by other bodies. Following the studies which were made from an engineering and economic standpoint in those years it was felt that the project would be of great benefit to the economy of Canada. That view has been strengthened: by the development of natural resources which have taken place since that time.
It was on the basis of those studies, both economic and engineering, that two governments of this country, one headed by a former prime minister, the late Lord Bennett, and1 the other headed by the former prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, entered into a treaty and an agreement with the United States for the joint development of the power and navigational facilities. I am sure that the studies which have been made clearly indicate that greater trade would flow on the St. Lawrence seaway because of this development-greater trade from the natural resources in certain parts of Canada, such as the iron ore deposits in Labrador and1 Quebec, and elsewhere-and also because of the great power development which would bring industry in its wake. Those are the main things that come to my mind at the moment.

Is it expected, for example,
that ocean freighters will come right up through the seaway system to Toronto, Windsor, Fort William and Port Arthur, or will there merely be transfers from oceangoing freighters to great lakes cargo vessels? Studies must have been made as to what is apt to happen to our traffic. If oceangoing vessels are to carry the freight right up to Fort William and Port Arthur, then of course that would affect very much the freight carried by the railways across Ontario. What is expected to follow from the construction of the seaway?

That is a rather difficult
question to answer. While the seaway, if developed in accordance with the plan, will thereafter be twenty-seven feet in depth, there are many ocean-going vessels that will not find it profitable to navigate the entire route because of the draft and because of the length of time it would take to go through the lakes. In that respect I do
Supply-Transport
not think a great deal of change will take place. But there are other vessels, such as trampers, that may find it economical to move right through the canal system up into the great lakes area, and if they do they probably will seek trade in that area. The studies which have been made indicated that it might be possible to bring grain in lake carriers right through to Montreal, unload there or at Quebec, Three Rivers, Sorel, places of that kind; then go on empty to the Seven Islands area; there pick up a return cargo of iron ore and come back through the canal systems. Of course ships will have to be built to accommodate that kind of cargo and that kind of trade. I understand that certain companies have plans and specifications in readiness in case the project is proceeded with.

I presume the iron ore would
be carried back to United States ports?

Or Canadian ports, if the
industrial development necessitated that movement on our shores.
Under present conditions most of the iron ore would go to United States lake ports.
Yes.

And I presume would be
carried in United States bottoms.
Not necessarily. The companies I had in mind a moment ago were Canadian.
Iron ore from the Mesabi range is carried in American bottoms.
It is also carried in Canadian boats, but what I had in mind a moment ago was that certain Canadian steamship companies already have plans in readiness for the movement of that ore.
What is the estimated cost of the St. Lawrence waterway, and what proportion of that cost is to be paid by Canada?

The latest estimate I have-* and of course I speak from memory-is in the neighbourhood of $860 million, of which Canada would be responsible for about $130 or $140 million. Mind you, that is after giving credit for the amounts we have spent on the Welland canal and the upper reaches of the lakes, and the power development.
How long would it take to complete the seaway?
It is estimated it would take about five years.

Is the Canadian government not having any engineering surveys made, or making any preparations of the kind for this

Supply-Transport
waterway? Apparently Canada is committed to the project, and is merely waiting for agreement by the United States. What steps are being taken by the government by way of preparation?

First of all, the surveys of which my hon. friend speaks have already been made. The plan is a single-stage control scheme that has been approved by provincial and federal engineers. That is already in existence at the plan stage. In the Department of Transport there has been established a special projects branch which will deal with the expropriation of the necessary lands and with all problems assigned to the federal government under the agreement. Beyond that I can say no more.
Is there any engineering work being done on the plan at the moment?
No.
Is any engineering firm doing any work on it at the moment?
No. There could not be any until the scheme had been approved between governments.
Has there been any arrangement made with any engineering firms for work on the seaway?
No.
The government is just sitting and doing nothing whatever about these plans in the meantime.

No, the government is not just sitting. The government is holding itself ready, as I stated a moment ago, by the establishment in the department of a special projects division to deal with matters concerning expropriation of the land, and the moment the agreement is approved, if it is, by the United States government, it will have to be approved by this house. It will take some five or six years to complete the project, so there will be plenty of time to appoint engineers and to proceed with the work that concerns the federal government. There are many works concerning provincial governments in connection with the joint project.

Has the government had
any reports from engineering firms on this project?
No.
And has no engineering firms engaged to work on it?

No, but it has a chief engineer in the department whose business for the last twenty-five years has been to deal specifically with the St. Lawrence waterway. He has

kept himself well informed, is in contact with the United States authorities on the other side, and is quite familiar with the project as a whole.
I hate to break up this conversation, but I have been waiting anxiously to find out whether the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra is for or against the project.
I have been trying to keep an open mind and get the facts.

I have not kept an open mind about it, and I definitely want to put that on the record. I also want to make it quite clear that I am speaking for myself on this occasion. Other members of this group may have other opinions. They live in other parts of the country.
The St. Lawrence waterway project is not a new one. During the last twenty-five years I have heard some very active discussions about it. So far as my memory serves me there has always been total opposition to this project on the part of the maritime provinces. The wisdom of those who were opposing it twenty-five years ago has been well demonstrated to me since coming to this house. The government of the United States was never very much interested in completing this project until the development of the iron ore deposits in Labrador and Ungava took place. With that field of raw material available, the United States is in a great rush to have this project completed.
In his brief statement the minister made it quite clear, in so far as Canada is concerned, the thinking on this project, from either a transportation or an economic aspect, ceases completely at Montreal. No thought has been given beyond Montreal at all. The minister clearly stated that once this waterway was opened it would mean that a certain type of ship could land a cargo of grain in Montreal, then the boat could pick up a cargo of iron ore and take it back to the United States or to other parts of Canada. I am not blaming the minister, but that clearly indicates that the minister has taken the advice of his engineers and departmental officials, and he is merely repeating what he has heard in discussing the subject. There is hardly any thought on the subject east of Montreal. I should like to remind the minister that there are four provinces east of Montreal. People live there, work there and pay taxes; and they should be given some consideration.
What does this development mean to the maritime provinces? It means that this mode of transportation will replace transportation by railroad. I am glad to note

that the railroad workers are objecting to it in their briefs. They know what will happen. The whole development is designed to make cheaper transportation available, and it is designed to tap the Labrador resources for the benefit of the United States. I also oppose it from that angle, that it is going to mean a curtailment of transportation and the laying off of railroad workers. The most important objection I have to it is that it is tapping resources in Canada, and making them available cheaply to the United States when they should have been developed by Canada.
Then, I am concerned about the coal industry of the maritimes. Twenty or twenty-five years ago I heard that the only reason that we have an economic market for maritime coal in Quebec is because there is no water route into that market from the United States coal fields. The development of the St. Lawrence waterway would mean that United States coal could be shipped in to replace that portion of the Quebec market now supplied by the Nova Scotia industry. The whole trend of thought, so far as the development of Canada is concerned, has been and still is detrimental to the maritime provinces. When the question of decentralization was being discussed, I mentioned the St. Lawrence waterway briefly. The Prime Minister wanted to know whether I was for it or against it. I am very definitely against it, because clearly no thinking is being done east of Montreal. The whole trend is to forget the eastern part of the country. Every economic development that has taken place has been designed, not to promote the welfare of the maritimes but to cripple what is already established there.
This cheap means of transportation means the carrying of iron ore up the St. Lawrence to the United States, when it might have been shipped by rail. This would mean that railroad workers would be laid off east of Montreal, and that would result in a continuation of the centralization of industry in the central part of Canada and the United States. In discussing this project not long ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce publicly stated that if the St. Lawrence waterway is not developed some of the steel plants in the central United States and central Canada might have to shift to the Atlantic seaboard. That is exactly what I have been advocating. With ore available in that part of the country, with about ten per cent of the population unemployed in that area now, with coal available, there should be an expansion of the steel industry in that area.	The minister makes it quite
Supply-Transport
clear that that is the thing he is trying tc prevent by the development of the St. Lawrence waterway. As a representative of the maritimes, I am not prepared to vote the Canadian taxpayers'' money to further a project that has as its only purpose the crippling of that part of the country which I represent. I agree with the member for Vancouver-Quadra when he said that a committee should be appointed, either a committee of this house or a commission of some kind, for the purpose of examining the economic aspect of this particular project, not as to its effect on the Toronto-Montreal area but as to its effect on the area from Vancouver to Newfoundland.
I am afraid that most of the thinking on any of the economic developments of the future, now as in the past, ceases at Montreal. Canada seems to be from Montreal to the other side of the Ontario border. So far as I am concerned, Mr. Chairman, I want to state emphatically that I think a committee of some kind should be set up to ascertain all the facts in connection with this project, and . see that it is developed to the best advantage of the whole of Canada, not just a section of Canada. I am going to continue to oppose it. This afternoon the minister made it quite clear that the thinking stops at Montreal. I believe the time has come when members of this house who represent ridings east of Montreal should be asserting themselves on matters of this kind. If they do not the result will be destruction of the part of the country from which they come.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the hon. member would not want to attempt to have me say things that are not on the record, and which I certainly did not say in my opening remarks on this item. In the first place, we are discussing an item that has nothing to do with the St. Lawrence waterway. This is an item of $10,000 covering St. Lawrence ship canal surveys and investigations. When the St. Lawrence waterway is up for discussion in this house, that will be the time for the house to decide whether or not it is advisable to have a committee to discuss the economic, engineering or other aspects of it. If the hon. member is of the opinion that I believe the thinking begins and stops at Montreal, he is entirely mistaken. If he believes that I am echoing the views of the officers of the Department of Transport, he is also entirely mistaken. I was born with this question, and I have discussed it for years. The thinking of the officers in the department has had no influence, in so far as my opinions on the project are concerned. My friend has discussed it from one point of view, that is from the navigational point of

Supply-Transport
view. But that is only a small part of the advantages which are to be derived from this project. Many of the advantages, and perhaps the greatest-although I do not say they are- are the advantages 'arising out of the power development. Surely it must be the wish of members of parliament to see to it that when power is available in the country it should be developed because of the great benefits and advantages that will be derived not only by the people residing in the immediate area where the power will be developed but by the nation as a whole.
I think that the thinking of my hon. friend is that which existed in this country twenty-five or fifty years ago. But that thinking has changed today. From one part of Canada to the other, where there are power and navigational facilities that can be developed, I believe they should be developed. I do not think, as my hon. friend seems to believe, that this development will have the effect he thinks it will have upon the maritime provinces; because the arguments he used are exactly the same arguments which were used against the 14-foot draft canals on the St. Lawrence many years ago. In those days the railways were drastically opposed to the development of those canals because they said it would take traffic away from them. The point is that it has brought traffic to the railways and today you find both the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway of one mind on this development because unquestionably it cannot do anything else but bring great benefit to Canada.

I should like to ask the minister one question. Can he tell me briefly what benefits the development of the St. Lawrence is going to bring to the maritime provinces, either from a power standpoint or in the development of any section of the maritimes?

The point my hon. friend was making was that we should not do this in central Canada because it would be detrimental to the maritime provinces. I am not admitting that it is detrimental to the maritime provinces. If my hon. friend states that it is, it would be for him to substantiate that assertion.
The minister has not refuted anything I said.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is good for all Canada.

Without necessarily associating myself completely with the hon. member for Cape Breton South in his statement that all thinking ceases at Montreal, I want to associate myself with him by saying that I believe that the development of the St.

Lawrence waterway as a power-plus-navigation project would be extremely detrimental to the maritime provinces. I do not believe that the hon. member for Cape Breton South is speaking in the language of twenty-five years ago when he makes that statement. I think he is speaking in the language of today. I believe that is an opinion that is shared by all people of all parties in the maritimes. There are two phases to this problem. The minister has stressed the necessity for power development. *With that I do not think anyone will quarrel. It is true' that it will probably add to the industrial expansion of elephantine proportion that the central provinces are enjoying today, and that they will become more and more developed industrially, perhaps at some expense to the rest of Canada. But with that we cannot quarrel. If it is in the nature of events for the industrial development to be centred here because of the development of power, that is one thing. But I think that the situation is confused because, despite the statement of the minister and his emphasis on power, he will agree that the two were taken together and that any surveys which have been made and anything which has been done heretofore have been in contemplation of both navigation and power. If the minister would assure this committee that any development that will take place on the St. Lawrence will be that of power alone, without development of navigation, then at least I do not think we as Canadians can conscientiously oppose it, because what is for the good of part of Canada is probably good for the whole development. But there can be no question in the world that the development of navigation on the St. Lawrence, as contemplated by some of the idealists, would be extremely detrimental to the maritimes. You have the outports there which you used during the time of war-Halifax, Saint John and other eastern Canadian ports-which suffer enough today from lack of traffic and which would be prejudiced still more if this development should take place.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South suggested that there would be a migration of steel. I have here the exact statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He says that the St. Lawrence waterway must be built and that without this development the steel industry now centred on the great lakes will have to migrate to the Atlantic coast.
What a tragedy that would be! Just imagine, Mr. Chairman, the steel industry having to migrate to the Atlantic coast! Why, it would be a terrible thing, would it not? It would be a tragedy apparently beyond compare, in the minds of some people. I do not

think it would be so devastating. No one of course suggests or believes that it would migrate to the coast. There still would be plenty of room for development of the steel industry on the great lakes. But certainly a healthy expansion of the steel industry on the Atlantic coast would be extremely desirable. I think any fair-minded Canadian would agree with that statement. I must say that I found people from Ontario, Quebec and all parts of Canada perfectly fair in their attitudes towards this matter, at least in their statements and in their thinking; although when it comes to a practical application of it, sometimes it does not work out in quite the same way. We have on the east coast the ore, the gypsum and the coal and there should be established a steel industry much larger than the one we have today, one which can enjoy export markets, which will provide a market for our agricultural products. We have the Atlantic ports which, as I say, will suffer because of this canal and which today offer us some market.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Surely.
Will he say how the maritime provinces will suffer because of this development?	.
How?
Yes.

Because I am sure it will prejudice shipments going through the ports of Halifax, Saint John, Sydney and other Canadian ports; because railway traffic would diminish. Therefore railway freight rates would be increased and traffic which we ship today in and out would pay heavier costs. It would1 prejudice the steel industry now situated in Sydney and would prevent the natural and proper expansion of that industry which would take place if it were not for the further development of this canal. As the hon. member for Cape Breton South said, certainly it is a strange coincidence that we have this impetus today on the development of the canal once you find the iron ore in Labrador. There can be little doubt but that there is some association between the two. The emphasis which is placed on that now and the haste with which it is considered has some relationship to the fact that this ore will now be taken to central Canadian points and on the great lakes rather than manufactured on the Atlantic coast.
And to United States ports.

Yes, and to United States ports, probably on the great lakes.
Supply-Transport
We have heard suggestions to the effect that this canal is essential to the development of our war effort. Let us not have that, Mr. Chairman. If this canal is essential to the development of the industrial life of Canada, that is one thing. But let us not camouflage it behind statements associating it with essentiality to our war effort. Any war effort that this country may make will be based on the sacrifice of the people and the desire to serve, as it has been in the past two wars, and will have no relationship whatsoever to the development of this canal.
As the minister knows, the transportation problems of the maritimes are extremely serious. We have the fact now that our long, attenuated Canadian National system, built because of apprehended war seventy-five years ago, is casting a heavier burden on transportation in the maritimes than it properly should cast. Certainly any taking away of traffic from it would simply add to that burden. If, as and when proper surveys are made, and it is determined that this project must go ahead, I suggest that there should be a division between the navigation and the power development, that we should be given the information as to what would be the cost of the potential power developments on the river and what would be-and of course this is easily available, I presume- the power development. I am sure that could be proven to be economically feasible. I should also like to know what would be the additional cost of providing navigation facilities necessary for modern traffic and what would be the potential traffic using those facilities. When that information is available, this committee would then be in a position to pass some independent judgment on the matter. It is all right for the minister to say that this is five years in contemplation. It is nothing of the kind. We are voting now an estimate of $10,000 for preliminary surveys and we are at least to some extent approving of the principle of at least investigating it. Let us investigate, Mr. Chairman. Let us have it clearly understood in this house that before any investigations are summarized, before any judgments are passed thereon, the whole matter will be considered by a competent committee of this house and a decision arrived' at on the basis of the national benefit to this country, and not of any sectional advantage which may develop therefrom.

I think perhaps I might again call the attention of the committee and of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken to the fact that he is under an entire misapprehension as to what we are voting at the moment. He seems to be of the opinion that

Supply-Transport
we are voting on the St. Lawrence seaway project. We are not. He has turned his whole argument in that direction.
In so far as the project itself is concerned, if the hon. member wants a breakdown of the cost and the traffic, that is easily available in the department, and I shall be glad to let him have that information if he so desires.
I would appreciate it.

But I should like to draw one or two things to his attention. First of all, he has been in this house before and this item has been up for at least five years. The sum of $10,000 has been voted for these surveys, and I have never heard him make any objection to this item, certainly not the vehement objection which he makes to it today.
If I may interrupt, I was here only once before, and the house dissolved so quickly that we did not vote these items, and that is why I did not have a chance to speak on it.

I remember that on one occasion during the consideration of my estimates, and at the very time that these items were up for discussion, my hon. friend spoke at great length on the Maritime Freight Kates Act. While he may have been here for a short time, I do know that he has not discussed it before. So that there will be no misunderstanding about it, let me assure him that the party of which he is a member has been strongly in favour of this project, and the government headed by the Right Hon, Mr. Bennett signed a treaty with the United States approving it. We are not discussing the treaty, and neither are we discussing the terms or the project. What we are doing is considering an item of $10,000 for ship canal surveys.
My hon. friend says that it is not essential for defence, and. laughs it off as if it were more or less a farce. Well, the joint board of defence, composed of both Americans and Canadians, have decided in their formal meetings that the development of the St. Lawrence waterway is essential for the defence of this country. A former president of the United States has so stated, and so has the present President of the United States. The joint board of defence has declared that not only is it essential for the defence of this continent, but also it is essential from the point of view of the economy, and it is also essential from the point of view of power, because when there is in this country a province whose people state that unless they have power within the next four or five years they will have to close down, or at least curtail power facilities, and by inference industrial

advantages to that province, I do not think that any parliament can refuse to take cognizance of that fact. That is the case not only with reference to one province, but it is so with reference to two provinces where power shortage is acute. All of these surveys that have been made indicate clearly that this project is essential from the point of view of defence, from the point of view of economy, and from the point of view of power. But, Mr. Chairman, I should like to get back to the purpose of this vote, which after all is the small amount of $10,000 for the purpose of making surveys and investigations. After all, the United States is spending at least a million dollars for this very matter, for which we have in our estimates the small sum of $10,000. I do not know how it is that we got off on the discussion of a project which is in no way before the committee -under this item. If hon. members want to debate the question of the advisability of making the surveys, that is another matter altogether, but that in fact is what the item is about.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman. The minister has mentioned several times that we are not in order in discussing the St. Lawrence seaway, but I would like to point out to him that this item has to do with the St. Lawrence canal system, and I submit that we are perfectly in order in discussing the proposed changes in this system. There is no rule of the house that would prevent us from dis-cussing it on this particular item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No ruling has been made.

I agree with the hon.
member for Vancouver-Quadra. I think the minister would be ill advised to endeavour to get the Chair to rule that this matter should not be discussed now that it has been opened for discussion. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has said, it does provide the small amount of $10,000 for expenses in connection with the St. Lawrence ship canal surveys and investigations. It seems to me that that is what we are discussing.
I think the discussion this afternoon illustrates very clearly how difficult it is sometimes to reconcile various conflicting regional interests in this country. The hon. member for Annapolis-Kings said a few moments ago that if this were purely a power development plan, that would put a different complexion on it. But those of us who come from the prairie provinces are interested in this particular project, not only from the point of view of power, which we recognize as very important to central Canada, but also from the point of view of shipping. We

realize that the ports at the head of the lakes would become ocean ports, that ships that carry grain would be able to pass right from the doorstep, almost, of the grain producing areas of Canada across the ocean, without the transshipment of grain that is now essential, and we believe that should be an economic gain to our part of Canada. And so you see that these considerations very largely cross parties and more or less compel consideration of the problem, I hope, not from each of our sectional points of view, but from the economic welfare of the whole of Canada.
I do not think that we can stop the wheels of progress turning and moving forward. I think that a project of this description has to be considered from the point of view of what will ultimately benefit the whole of Canada. It is true that the great Ungava fields now being developed for iron ore may, I regret to say, see most of that ore shipped to the United States. If I read the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce aright the other day, when he spoke of the movement of the steel plants from the great lakes to the maritime coast, I do not think he was thinking of the maritime coast of Canada. I think he was thinking of moving these plants to the maritime coast of the United States.
Quite.

As a matter of fact, there are projects I think in New London, Connecticut, and in other places on the maritime coast of the United States for the establishment of huge steel mills there.
To my mind what we should have done years ago was to have laid out a national plan for the development of our economic resources so that our iron ore and other minerals, our gypsum and other resources, could have been fabricated in Canada, rather than exporting much of this raw material, as we have been doing, to the United States for a large number of years. But while governments may be to blame for that to some extent, let us not forget that Canadians who had the money and the power to undertake these projects are also blameworthy. If Canadian capital had been alive to the advantages that could accrue to it from the development of these resources, I do not think we would be discussing some of these problems in the manner in which they have been discussed this afternoon.
I do not think you can stand in the way of progress. I think that while every attempt must be made to assist the maritime region- the whole region, not only Nova Scotia or Cape Breton or New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island or Newfoundland separately
Supply-Transport
-this government should be placing before the house projects and plans for the development of the whole of the maritime area. Then perhaps we should not be thinking in the terms in which the hon. members for Cape Breton South and Annapolis-Kings are bound to think this afternoon.
I do not blame them for thinking the way they were thinking. They think very much as we do in the prairie provinces, that we have not industries there that we should have. I want to see industries established on the prairies; I want to see our water power and irrigation projects developed there. I want to see the Saskatchewan river used, and the waters contained therein. I want to see a larger estimate than we have in the estimates this year for those things. I want to see the Outlook dam proceeded with, not only for irrigation but for power.
Byt all those projects are projects in the interests of all of Canada; because if we build up the economy of one part of Canada we shall indeed be assisting the economy of all parts of Canada. I agree that before we undertake the vast expenditures which are to be made in connection with this project-and the survey is a small thing-the matter must be gone into thoroughly by the house.
I was here some years ago when the agreement with the United States was discussed. I remember distinctly the discussion that took place at that time. I remember that all parties in the house, including opposition parties, were favourable to the development. Let us not forget that since the canals system of Canada was started many years ago or, shall I say, was developed-the Welland canal for example-we have built a large part of our share of that ship canal system. We have already a very large investment in the project.
While I have every sympathy-and of course this is an easy thing to say-with what has been said by the maritime members, yet from the point of view of the whole country I believe Canada would be wise to consider the pressing of this matter with the United States, so that we may have the power, so that we may have .shipping facilities, and so that this country may make great progress as a modern and progressive nation should make progress.

Mr. Chairman, for once I am glad "to be able to agree with everything the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has said. Representing as I do a constituency on the upper reaches of the St. Lawrence river, this matter of a St. Lawrence seaway has been uppermost in our minds for many years. I remember as a small boy hearing about it.

Supply-Transport
So when an hon. member from Nova Scotia says that the item today is for a preliminary survey, I wish to bring him up to date. I remember well when in 1927 a complete survey was being made under the Canadian chairmanship of the late General Charles Mitchell, then head of the school of practical science at the university of Toronto. I remember the fact that at that time he was working in closest co-operation with the United States army engineers. I believe it was from those surveys it was decided that the Barnhart island dam should be provided for the international section of the St. Lawrence system.
Nothing could more definitely typify the great waste of a great natural resource God has given Canada than to see the mighty waters of the St. Lawrence river flowing by our doors every second of each day, for 365 days in the year.	.

We also have water going by
our doors, in the South Saskatchewan river, that is going to waste.

Can you produce 1,100,000
horsepower of electrical energy at one place out in western Canada? Can you produce that out west? In the county of Leeds we will not benefit materially from the navigation end of the St. Lawrence seaway, but we will benefit tremendously from power development. We hope we are looking at this matter in a broader sense than that of just looking after our own interests. We realize that in bringing shipping of the world up to the head of the great lakes it would be of great advantage to this great dominion of ours. Every farmer in the west stands to benefit from it through lowered freight rates. The manufacturers in the east will also benefit. There is hardly a class or a community in Canada that will not benefit materially.
I have always believed in the old adage that what is good for the whole is good for any one part. I cannot see how the argument we have just heard from the maritime provinces is valid. They say that they fear they will lose their shipping. They will still get the shipping they get now during four months of the year-and that is a virtual monopoly and will continue to get it anyway, when the ports are closed on the St. Lawrence. No system has been devised of keeping the great lakes ports open twelve months of the year.
Then, the great ore deposits in Labrador and northeastern Quebec cannot be properly developed and utilized until the great smelters along the great lakes are utilized to the full, through the ore that will come from that section. We need only think of the tremendous amount of $360 million invested

in a railway to bring ore from the fields to Seven Islands harbour.
If we can believe what geologists tell us, the development in that Labrador and northeastern Quebec section represents the greatest iron ore find of the ages. Certainly Seven Islands harbour is much nearer Glace Bay and other ports of Nova Scotia than it is to any port on the great lakes. Naturally all the ore that will be necessary will find its way there, to Nova Scotia. Then, added to that, this vast ore body will be supplying smelters on the great lakes.
In spite of the evidence being given in the United States congress I am told on reliable authority that good grade iron ore is running out in the United States. We know the end is in sight in the great Minnesota Mesabi range. Is it conceivable that a great plan like this can be held up in Canada? We at present are seeing the actions of certain vested interests in our neighbour to the south of us, and I am afraid that some of the arguments I heard this afternoon in the committee sounded very much like the argument we hear to the south of us, in the capital of the great United States of America.

The maritime provinces
have shipped all the year round from Halifax.

I shall clarify what I meant.
I meant to say that there will be four months of the year in which the maritime provinces will have exclusive shipping.
In British Columbia we would have twelve months.

I do not think British
Columbia has anything to fear from the St. Lawrence deep waterways. Indeed, that province has everything to gain from it. I would plead therefore with the minister, in as strong language as I can use, that every conceivable consideration be given immediately, as a result of these surveys, and that through our Department of External Affairs strong representations be made to United States authorities to see that this long-kicked-about football is taken out of the realm of petty politics and placed where it should be placed, for the betterment and well-being of the Dominion of Canada and the United States.

Mr. Chairman,
apparently quite a debate is developing on this item. As some maritime members have made a few remarks, I should like to point out that this proposition is causing considerable worry in the maritime provinces. The hon. member who has just resumed his seat has stated that the St. Lawrence waterway must be completed. I do not take issue

with that, but I should like to point out the position in which the maritime provinces are placed.
It has been mentioned during the debate that ore can be carried from Labrador through the St. Lawrence seaway to the head of the lakes. I understand at the present time we are importing considerable steel from the United States. Where steel is manufactured in the central parts of Canada the necessary coal must be imported from the United States. I have always understood that the closer together you can get your ore and coal, the cheaper you can manufacture steel.
We have in the maritime provinces coal of a quality suitable for the manufacture of steel, and the iron ore is available for transportation by water, which transportation can be used twelve months in the year. Our coal cannot find a market any further west than Montreal. It seems logical to the maritime provinces that the ore available there should be manufactured into steel in the maritime provinces. If this ore is taken to the head of the lakes and manufactured into steel in the United States, that steel will be imported back into Canada at a cost 25 per cent greater than it could be manufactured here. It is not easy to explain this issue in the maritime provinces.
Mention has been made of the power development. Any power that has been developed in my province has been developed by the people of New Brunswick, not by the federal government. I do not see how I can go back to the maritime provinces and justify assistance by the federal government for the development of power in the central provinces. I feel that those provinces are in a much better financial position to develop their own power than we are in New Brunswick.
There is a possible power development in my own county, the Passamaquoddy development, which has been under discussion for about twenty years. There does not seem to be the same interest taken in that power development as is taken in the St. Lawrence, and I wonder why. This is a tidal development and there would be no danger of drought or floods, no valuable property would be flooded and therefore no damages would have to be paid. This power development has a potential capacity of over one million horsepower, as great as the potential capacity of the St. Lawrence power development.
When consideration is given to the coal and the facilities for the manufacture of steel that we have, to the population available, which in many cases has had to leave
Supply-Transport
in order to get work in other parts of Canada, I think it will be seen that it is time that serious consideration was given to that part of Canada. I am sure that the arguments that have been used by hon. members from the maritime provinces will meet with the approval of the people down there.
I want to go on record as supporting anything of a general nature that will benefit all Canada, but I do feel that other parts of the country should receive the same consideration. With this ore available I believe that the logical place to manufacture it into steel is the maritime provinces. It is much cheaper to transport a finished product than it is to transport raw material. The materials and the manufacturing know-how are available there and I feel that the maritime provinces are perfectly justified in asking that this industry should be established in that part of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I should
like to say a word or two on this subject which seems to have caused so much controversy among the members of the house. They appear to be divided according to the part of the country in which they live, and I think that is deplorable. I am in favour of the development of the St. Lawrence project in both its power and transportation aspects.
I do not believe that the government under whose authority this development will take place will	allow the development to
adversely affect any other part of Canada. Surely that is not the way the development of Canada should be visualized. It is unthinkable that this addition to the wealth of Canada should be allowed to militate against either the maritime provinces or British Columbia. That can not happen if we have a government that is thinking in terms of Canada and not in terms of local areas and certain vested interests in those areas. That is the way in which this great national development must be approached.
I do not think the plight of the maritime provinces could be any worse than it is now no matter what development takes place in other parts of Canada. I think those maritime members who oppose the development of the St. Lawrence project are standing in their own light when they argue that it would be detrimental to the interests of the maritime provinces. The members on the government side who take that position surely must have little faith in the government they support. If I had so little faith in a government I would not support it at all because it would not be worthy of support
It seems to me that that is a fundamental principle. This parliament is dealing with

Supply-Transport
the affairs of Canada and we must have in mind the welfare of the Canadian people, no matter in what part of the country they reside. We should not permit favourable circumstances in one part of the country to improve the position only of those who live in that section of the country. What would one think of parents who would promote the interests of one member of the family in such a way as to hurt the interests of the other members? You would think they were mighty poor parents, would you not? I would say this is a mighty poor government if, by promoting the development of one part of Canada, it would allow another part to be impoverished. I hope that the government will go ahead with this project in conjunction with the government of the United States, and that it does so with all speed. In the same way I hope that the government will see to it that neither the maritime provinces on the east nor the maritime province on the west are any worse off, and not only no worse off but possibly much better because this development has taken place in central Canada and because of this great addition to the wealth of our country.

As a member from New Brunswick, one of the maritime provinces, I am not opposed to the St. Lawrence waterway development. I think that the whole of Canada will receive some benefit from it. No doubt it will have some repercussions on our international trade so far as the eastern Canada seaboard ports are concerned. I do not share the same view as some others that the mining development of Labrador should be concentrated so that we might become an exporting country in the finished steel product. I suppose we produce about two-thirds of the steel we consume in Canada today, if I am not mistaken as to my figures. Through the development of Labrador we might reach a point where we could produce sufficient in Canada to satisfy our own needs and become an exporting country, but I wish to point out, following the idea of the last speaker, that when it comes to handing out public funds for the development of these great resources we in New Brunswick would say:	Please pass
the dish around a little so that we may have a helping too.

I did not know the question of the St. Lawrence waterway was likely to come up under the present item. If I had known, there is a good deal of material that I might have placed before the house on the question of the St. Lawrence waterway. About all I want to say at the present time is that I am not against the St. Lawrence waterway having regard to the conditions

under which it has been inaugurated, and the conditions which have been made known to this country in the last four or five years. Twenty years ago, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South said, the mining and steel industries of Nova Scotia were against the inauguration of the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway extending across the United States border. The reason was that they thought their coal could not compete with United States coal. I have had a little experience in this matter.
Some years ago I acted on a commission. At that time the officials of the Dominion Coal Company raised the question of the St. Lawrence waterway. They advanced arguments against the deepening and construction of the St. Lawrence waterway, especially across the United States border. I told them at that time that we would have to give the matter much more consideration, that we did not know enough about it, and that perhaps it was not within the terms of reference. Lo and behold, however, we had meetings with the United States coal operators. The coal that comes into Canada comes mostly from West Virginia and Pennsylvania, and West Virginia and Pennsylvania will not be tapped by the St. (Lawrence waterway. The coal operators in the United States came before our commission and were absolutely against the St. Lawrence waterway for the reason that if it were built they could not compete with Nova Scotia coal.
When our friends in the Nova Scotia coal industry heard this argument they changed front and began to see the light as they should have seen it years ago. Coal export from the maritime provinces to the central provinces of Canada takes place in large quantity during the summer months up the St. Lawrence river to Montreal and farther west. With the aid of certain subventions and tariff protection, plus the fact that the rates were very cheap some years ago, they were practically able to compete with coal coming from the United States. Therefore, so far as the coal industry of Nova Scotia is concerned, the St. Lawrence waterway is going to permit them to ship their coal farther west than they do at the present time. The large barges that leave Sydney, Glace bay, Pictou or the other mining places from which coal is shipped, will have a greater opportunity to go farther inland, and therefore will be able to compete with United States coal more successfully than they can at the present time.
With respect to some of the inland mines, the situation may be a little different but they will ship no less coal in the wintertime than they will when the St. Lawrence is open

because practically all their shipments of coal are by rail from Springhill and certain other mines. I have nothing to say about the shipment of steel. It has always been thought also that the deepening and extension of the St. Lawrence waterway would injure shipping' in the port of Halifax. The other day I put a question on the order paper as to how many bushels or tons of wheat are shipped overseas from Halifax in the summer months when the St. Lawrence is open and how many are shipped in the winter months when it is closed to navigation. The amount of wheat shipped overseas from Halifax at the present time in the summer months is practically negligible. The great bulk is shipped in the winter months when the St. Lawrence is closed. Wheat that is shipped from Halifax in the summer months is mostly taken on as ballast by ships coming in there, and is not generally loaded there by ships coming to this country for wheat.
With regard to the shipment of steel from Sydney, as a matter of fact most of that goes by rail because that is the best way to ship it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member who said that we should approach matters of this kind from the Canadian viewpoint. I am from Cape Breton, and you can call me a maritimer if you like. I agree with everything that gentleman has said, except that we are in a sorry mess down in our part of the country. I want to tell this house that we are as well off in the parts of Nova Scotia with which I am acquainted as the people in any part of this country. We are making as good a living and we are, I hope, living as good lives as most of the other people. We have a good standard of living. I am not saying anything about the maritimes, because I do not know enough about them to ascertain whether or not they are in a sorry plight.
I do not know whether or not this subject should be mentioned now, although I intended mentioning it at some time, but it seems some mention has been made of the iron ore from Labrador. Someone has said that we do not do any thinking in our country east of Montreal. I have been giving this subject of the Labrador iron ore some thought. From the Department of Transport I obtained a map and a plan of that part of the country, including Labrador, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and the St. Lawrence river. I have not that map before me, but I should like to put on the record some facts concerning the distances from the source of this ore to various places in Canada and the United States. The distance between the source of this ore and the strait of Canso is very short. I have a proposition to make, not to the Minister of Transport but
Supply-Transport
to the minister who is looking after the industries of this country today. I would ask him to consider the possibility of establishing a steel industry on the shores of the strait of Canso. We have a harbour to the south which is open in the wintertime, and as good a harbour to the north as there is on the Atlantic coast. The iron ore could be brought in, and we have the finest coal available right there for the making of steel. We have the tremendous deposits of the Dominion Steel Corporation, who are making steel now. It would not interfere one iota with the production of the Dominion Steel Company or any other company we have in this country.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member must realize he is getting rather far afield.

I did say that, but this question was brought up by other hon. members in this house who were allowed to continue. I said that I had not intended going into this question, and as a matter of fact I was going to object when this debate started. I did not think this was the proper place to talk about the St. Lawrence waterway. However, the St. Lawrence waterway and this iron ore in Labrador were tied together. One objection to the St. Lawrence waterway was that we were not going to be able to utilize our own iron ore from Labrador in the province of Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Since the hon.
member has provided this explanation, he may continue. I thought the discussion of the St. Lawrence waterway had been permitted as incidental to the matter under discussion. When the hon. member began discussing the coal industry generally, I thought he was getting rather far afield.

One objection to the
St. Lawrence waterway was that it was going to interfere with our coal industry in the maritime provinces. I am not answering that objection, but I am putting forth my own views. I know something about this subject, because I made some study of it, not yesterday or the day before but some years ago. I hope that the minister in charge of production will read my remarks in Hansard tomorrow. I was going to speak on this subject during the budget debate, but I did not want to let this opportunity pass without showing that the people of this country are thinking about the maritime provinces. They are thinking of ways and means by which the iron ore from Labrador may be utilized right on the island of Cape Breton.
I am not asking that this be a government undertaking, Mr. Chairman. Today there is a large amount of capital in Great Britain

Supp ly-Transport
and the United States. The steel industry was taken away from the industrialists in Great Britain, and I understand a large amount of that capital would be available for investment in the steel industry in this country. There is something to which the good minister might give his attention. We are not looking to the government to build this industry. Governments have been building too many things in this country. The people have been too lazy to look around, or else they did not have enough vision to look after this industrialization.
Mr. Chairman, when the manufacture of steel was first started in this country by the Steel Company of Canada and the Dominion Steel Company, the government gave them assistance in the form of a bounty on steel rods that were to be used in the manufacture of other products in Canada. This bounty was continued until 1910 when Mr. Fielding eliminated it. The steel companies have received other forms of assistance, but all I would ask is for the minister to put this picture before some of the moneyed people in the United States, Great Britain or Canada.
Again I suppose it is not according to common sense or the rules of the house to say anything here about the strait of Canso. Whether the causeway-and that is what should be built-is built across the strait of Canso or not, this problem about which I am talking is absolutely feasible. If the causeway were built, it would mean a better harbour at that point. I should like to say again that we have free and easy access by water from the strait of Canso to Belle Isle. We have easy transportation from the strait of Canso to any part of the world. Of course I am going to take this matter up further with the good minister but I thought at this stage, when people are saying that there is no thinking about it, and that nothing is being thought about Nova Scotia, I should point out that, whether their ideas are right or not or whether they have any common sense behind them or not, there are in this chamber some people who are thinking about our own people in our own country down there.

I do not want to add anything to what I have already said on this subject, but I want to make a brief reply to the exception that the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond took to my remarks with regard to economic conditions in the maritimes.
I did not say anything about the maritime provinces. I was referring to the place I know about, the island of Cape Breton.

I was not quite as parochial as the hon.. member for Inverness-Richmond. I included the whole of the maritimes; and I am not speaking from hearsay. As the hon. gentleman may know, I had the honour and the good fortune to be born in the maritime provinces. I left my home in Prince Edward Island, the most beautiful of the maritime provinces, and sought my livelihood in other parts of this great country. If my leaving the maritimes were just an isolated case that would not prove anything. But for the last seventy-five years at least the great majority of the boys and girls born in those provinces have left them and have added their wealth of brain and brawn not only to other parts of this Canada of ours but to the United States as well,-of course to the great advantage of those other parts of Canada and to the United States. There can be no doubt that the maritime provinces have suffered in their economic development because of the concentration of business in the two central provinces.

I just wish to say that the sooner the St. Lawrence project can be finished, the better we shall be pleased. As to this small item, I hope that we may pass it as soon as we may after giving everyone a chance to express any views that he may wish to express. I believe that what helps one part of Canada must help all of Canada. I have no objection to helping my good friends in Quebec and Ontario to develop their provinces into a more powerful area. I think that is entirely in the best interests of Alberta.

I had not intended taking part in this debate at all, and I would not do so had it not been for one or two remarks made by the hon. member for Leeds. I agree with the minister that this is not the proper place to discuss these waterways. However, the hon. member for Leeds said that he saw a great deal of water going to waste down the St. Lawrence river every day. I wish the hon. member would come out west. We in the southern part of Alberta could show him a great deal of water that has been going to waste for years. We could have used that water. I believe that any water that goes to the sea without being used is a public waste. We could have used plenty of that water around the Medicine Hat area perhaps, as the hon. member for Leeds has said.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, may I say that if the hon. member had been in the house the other night when I was speaking about the $65 million payment to the western farmers, he would know that I mentioned that very point; I said that money should be used on the development of the waters of the west.
fMr. Carroll.]
I am glad the hon. member raised that point about the $65 million to the western farmers because he is one member who voted against that and he spoke against it too, if my memory serves me correctly.
That is because it was a handout.
I imagine that if the hon. member for Comox-Alberni who has just interrupted could ship some logs down the St. Lawrence waterways free, he would be quite in agreement with it.
I would pay whatever the tariff was.

That is good. However, I think that the development of this project would assist in the development of all of Canada. I am sure that every western member would want to see the development of this project, and I am sure it will have our support.
May I ask the minister once again whether he will give consideration to having this question studied by the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines?
What question?

Particularly just what the
effect of the seaway would be on our transportation system. As he will have seen from the discussion this afternoon, there is intense interest in the whole subject. One does not often see a debate flare up as has the debate this afternoon. There is no doubt that one of these days this question will be coming before the house, perhaps in great haste. I think the reasonable thing to do is to have the question considered by the standing committee of the house so that we would at least get a background of information. We could hear representations from the various people who are interested, and in that way it would be far more likely that the house would eventually reach the best conclusion having regard to the interests of Canada. As a matter of fact, in that way we may prevent the hard feelings and controversy that would follow for many years if the scheme were put through in a rush, without consideration of that type being given to it.

I do not know what it is that I could refer to a committee, whether it be the railways and shipping committee or the railways, canals and telegraph lines committee. Certainly it is not anything that is under this item. I would not be disposed to refer to a committee the subject matter of this discussion because it is not before the house. When the subject is before the house, I am sure the house will want to have it studied by a committee such as the one
Supply-Transport
my hon. friend has in mind. If the project is approved by the United States congress, then of necessity it must come before the House of Commons, where it will be submitted to a committee. If it is not approved, then this government will have to indicate what its policy is.
I had in mind a study of the impact of the St. Lawrence seaway on the transportation system of Canada. I think that sums up the thought I had in mind.

Item agreed to.
Marine services-
476. Marine services administration, including agencies, $513,944.

May I draw the attention of the minister to a situation which has occurred on the west coast since the introduction of the amendments to the Canada Shipping Act providing additional means for the safety of life at sea. At the time I called attention to the danger of the curtailment of services to some of the smaller islands lying between Vancouver island and the mainland.
