I regret to say that my forecast has proved to be only too accurate and that there has been a considerable curtailment of the steamship services between Vancouver island and the gulf islands, and between the mainland of British Columbia, from the port of Vancouver, and those same gulf islands, a situation which is causing considerable hardship upon the residents of those small islands. It has been necessary for the Canadian Pacific Railway to take off one of their older ships and to curtail their services because it would not justify that company to go to the expense of remodelling the ship. Actually, the service between the gulf islands and Vancouver island and the mainland is totally inadequate and is less today than it has been for the last sixty years. If this condition has not been brought before the minister's department I would appreciate it very much if it might be looked into to see whether something could be done to assist in the provision of a better service for the gulf islands.

The subject to which my
hon. friend refers was brought to my attention by a delegation from one of the operating companies affected. They had been in communication with the maritime commission on the matter of the service, and they indicated to me, and to the commission I believe, that unless they received a subsidy they would have to curtail their services in the northern part of the run. All I could indicate to them at the time when they did come-the decision of the maritime commission had not yet been handed down-was

Supply-Transport
that I would pass along to the commission their representations, because the commission is charged with the responsibility of deciding whether or not a subsidy is warranted. In view of what my hon. friend has said, if the commission had not yet handed down their decision, I shall see that his observations are brought to their attention.
Thank you very much.

Item agreed to.
479. Construction or acquisition of vessels, as detailed in the estimates-capital, $2,254,800.

Can we get a little information about this item? In the past there has been a good deal of discussion regarding the provision of a coastguard service. During the last year we have seen very definite steps taken in the direction of co-ordinating the existing services. I should like to express my appreciation, on behalf of the people of the west coast of British Columbia, for the services which have been rendered during the last year, and which have been more effective owing to the co-ordination which has taken place. I understand that provision is being made to extend the service still further. Is that correct?

Yes. First of all, the matter is no longer under my jurisdiction. Up until last year it was; but now, because of the recommendation of the commission, it is no longer my responsibility. It is the responsibility of the Minister of National Defence.
I am very happy to hear my hon. friend speak thus, because his colleague from Anna-polis-Kings spoke very strongly last night about the lack of a coastguard service. I wish the hon. member for Nanaimo would indicate to the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings what the position is on the west coast.
I do not know anything about the east coast.

What he does know-and I thank him for having said so-is that because of the co-ordination of services which was instituted last year, a new service has been established under the aegis of the Royal Canadian Air Force, namely, the search and rescue division. That division will coordinate all of the ships in all of the departments, together with national defence vessels, and ships privately operated. I have a detailed statement here of the instructions that have gone out to each of the departments and to each of the agencies concerned, so that there will be complete co-operation.
I think my hon. friend deserves some credit for the interest which he has taken in this in the last few years, and we have given careful consideration to the representations which came to us from the west
coast, as well as to the statements which he made from time to time in the house. I would be glad to show him this statement. It is rather lengthy to put on record, but it certainly would indicate to him the attention which the interdepartmental committee on search and rescue gave to this very vital problem.
Just one question on that: does that coastguard service apply to inland lakes as well?

Yes, it does, because one of the stations designated in the plan is at Trenton. Therefore it has to do with casualties and ships in distress on the lakes as well. May I answer the questions that my hon. friend asked some time ago in connection with the Rideau canal. He inquired as to the number of boats that passed through the locks of the Rideau canal. I have not the figures for 1950, but the total for 1949 is 18,472. Then he inquired as to the total amount of revenue on the Welland canal. It is $715,402. The total amount of the Rideau canal is $21,690. Then he asked for the breakdown in each case. In the latter it is $8,358 for land; $2,347 for water power; $4,521 for private line service; $2,885 living quarters and $110 for winterizing. Other revenue which is not broken down is $3,467. I think that makes the total.

Has the minister available there the list of ships to which he made reference this afternoon, and also last night, which would co-ordinate within this service? I am talking about the ships under his department. I know he has that, and possibly he has them for the other departments as well.

All the ships under my department, and there are some fifty, are subject to call, no matter where they may be, by direction from the R.C.A.F. or the search and rescue co-ordination division, and all of the ships of the other departments of the government, such as those of the mounted police, the fishing vessels of the Department of Fisheries, and I think the hydrographic service, and all naval vessels. They are subject to the same call as are our own vessels. That makes a substantial total which I have not at my fingertips, but it is quite a considerable number.
Of the fifty, how many are on the east coast? Can the minister give us that information?
Yes. I will get it in a moment. Can we go on, and I shall let the hon. member have it?
Item agreed to.

Aids to navigation-
480. Administration, operation and maintenance, $4,215,904.
There is quite a substantial increase on this item. Can the minister explain the reason for it?

This item is now a consolidation of the former item bearing the same name, plus the maintenance and repairs to wharves and the breaking of ice in Thunder bay, in accordance with a new policy in treasury board where a division of capital and maintenance and operation are now given to the house in two votes. That is the reason why one finds these two votes here.
The reason for the increase is that there have been increases in salaries and wages. Of the $199,644 increase, $152,650 is for increases in salaries and wages, and the other main item to make up the $199,000 is one of $36,400, an increase in the cost of materials and supplies.
I should like to say a word on this item about aids to navigation.

May I be permitted to answer the question of the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings? There are seven ships at the Dartmouth agency, two at the Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, agency, and three at the Saint John, New Brunswick, agency. That makes twelve ships.

This item of aids to navigation is of great interest not only to mariners, properly so-called, but to the fishermen who gain their livelihood by fishing along the shores of the Atlantic coast. From time to time we receive from the fishermen suggestions as to improvements which can be made to the inshore markers, buoys and lights, which they believe are necessary for the safety of their operations.
It has been my experience that the co-operation and interest of the officials of the department who deal with this particular matter have been of the highest order. Apparently they realize the importance of the matter to these fishermen, and in every instance they try to deal in a helpful manner with any suggestions made.
I notice that this item shows a small increase. However, it has been my experience already this year that suggestions which have been made with respect to possible improvements in aids to navigation have been met with the suggestion that the necessity for economy in departmental operations makes it difficult to give consideration to these matters, as has been possible in many instances before.
Supply-Transport
I know we are all interested in the practising of economy and we would hope that the ordinary expenditure in the Department of Transport and all other departments might be reasonably curtailed. However, I would impress upon the minister and the committee the false economy that would result from any unreasonable cutting down in aids to navigation which are useful to fishermen. The safety of the men who carry out these arduous and dangerous tasks is of great importance, and I hope it will be possible to practise economy without in any way jeopardizing the essential requirements of the fishermen.
I know the minister will give this matter his close attention and I know from past experience that his officials, whose hearts are in the right place, will give every possible consideration to the needs of the men who go down to the sea in ships.
If this is the item under which we may deal with the operation of wharves it would be the appropriate time to make some observations concerning the Nanaimo assembly wharf.
There is a later item dealing with wharves.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to subscribe to what has been said by the hon. member for Halifax. I would bring to the minister's attention now a certain matter which would be before him for his consideration. In the bay of Fundy on the Nova Scotia coast extending, so I am told, all the way from Digby up to Spencer island in Minas basin there are no audible warnings or aids to navigation of any kind. In the event of fog it is impossible for shipping or fishing boats to take bearings, and it has been urged upon me that a whistle buoy of some sort should be placed upon those waters along that coast. It has been suggested this could be done most advantageously at Hall harbour, where there is a tidal rip, and where this buoy would be actuated at all times.
I do not know what the cost of such an installation would be, but I do not think it would be a major matter and I know it is something of great importance to all the fishermen who are operating small boats off the coast, as well as to tugboats servicing lumber boats. I would ask the minister to give this matter his attention.
I have asked my officers to look into it.
Item agreed to.

Supply-Transport Marine services-
483.	Operation and maintenance, including grants and contributions, as detailed in the estimates: rewards for saving life from vessels in distress; subsidies to salvage companies, and the payment of expenses, including excepted expenses, incurred in respect of Canadian distressed seamen as defined in section 296 of the Canada Shipping Act, $390,591.

At the last session there was considerable discussion as to whether there should be a full-time radio operator on ships plying the west coast. At that time the minister said the whole question would be reviewed by his department before the next session of the house. I presume that has been done. We had reports last December of on-the-spot surveys having been made of the whole question. Can the minister tell us the result of those surveys, and whether the department has reached any conclusion?

A survey has been made, but I have not yet had an opportunity to see the result of it. I have discussed some of the suggestions which came while the survey was in progress, but I have not yet had before me the complete report. Until that time I would rather withhold my comments.
Could the minister make an announcement in the matter within a reasonably short time?
I certainly will be able to reach a conclusion before the session ends, and will indicate in some way or other what the decision is.
Is this the item under which we discuss lifeboat services?
No; there is an item later in the estimates.

Item agreed to.
Marine services-
484.	Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment, $21,500.

I believe this would be the proper item under which to deal with the assembly wharf. I believe it was in 1933 that the wharf in Nanaimo was first built. It was then recommended that it should handle somewhere in the neighbourhood of 7,500,000 feet, but construction was never completed, so that at the present time it can handle only something less than 4 million feet. There are about twenty-two mills in the immediate neighbourhood, and there is at the present time a great demand for the full production of those mills.
The present situation however is that the capacity of the assembly wharf cannot take care of the production in the area. I am informed that if the wharf were extended so that two vessels could berth at the same
TMr. Chevrier.]
time the capacity would be increased four or five times the present amount. I know representations have been made to the government respecting the possibility of that extension. I understand however that the wharf is operated by the Johnston National Storage Company, either on lease or on some such terms. Would the minister state what those terms are, and whether the government receives more returns if a greater quantity of lumber is handled over the wharf?

I am afraid I cannot help my hon. friend much because in the Department of Transport we have nothing to do with the construction or repair of wharves. The construction and repairs of wharves are carried out by the Department of Public Works. We do have a small item of $5,000 for repairs to wharves of less than $50. The matter has probably been brought to the attention of the Minister of Public Works but if not I shall see that it is.
Can the minister indicate the terms under which the Johnston National Storage Company operate that wharf?

When the repairs are done or a wharf is constructed then it becomes part of our job to charge fees and the like. I am not familiar with the terms, but there probably is an agreement with the Johnston people and I will inquire what they are.
I should like to know whether there will be a greater return to the government if a greater volume is handled)?
I will see that the hon. member gets the information.

I should like to inquire about the number of boatmen employed. I notice the details on page 470 indicate 14 boatmen, but surely there must be other men employed in the lifeboat service. Are these just the ones under the civil service?

This particular item covers the construction or acquisition of buildings for shore-based lifeboats, one at Bay View, N.S., one at Bamfield, B.C., and the other at Clayoquot, B.C., and also improvements to the life-saving station at Clayoquot.
Are some of the boatmen under the civil service while others are under prevailing rates of pay?
The coxswains and engineers are under the civil service, and the prevailing rates men are under the department.
I gather that the boatmen are under prevailing rates?
That is right.
Are they listed here?
There are six in the Clayo-quot station and seven in the Bamfield station.
Are the coxswains and engineers under prevailing rates or under the civil service?
They are under the civil service superannuation fund.

I understand that some change has been made with regard to sick leave credits, that this privilege has been taken away from these men. I understand also that they were not given any intimation at all of this privilege being withdrawn and as a result one man has been billed for $49 for seven days' sick leave. The minister will appreciate that these men must go to town for medical services.

I am not familiar with the details of the case my hon. friend has in mind, but I understand from an officer of the department that all of the information has been provided to my hon. friend and that the case he has in mind can be remedied.

Item agreed to.
485.	Pilotage service, including authority for temporary recoverable advances not exceeding $13,000, $367,363.

What pilotage services are rendered in the port of Charlottetown? How many pilots are authorized to operate by the government? What are the qualifications necessary for a pilot's certificate? There has been some dispute among the pilots there and it might be of assistance if I could get that information.
The pilots of Charlottetown are not under the authority of the Department of Transport. They are under a local authority and operate their own business.
They can make any charge they wish?
I cannot answer that as I do not know the details of their bylaws and constitution.
Does the department permit any person to act as a master of a passenger vessel without having taken an examination and holding a master's certificate?

While that matter does not come under this item, the answer is no. Those who follow the calling of master or mate must obtain a certificate from the department if they are operating a vessel of over five tons. Of course if it is a rowboat or a small vessel or yacht under five tons there would be no requirement of that kind.
Supply-Transport
Have any changes been made in the regulations with regard to fires since the burning of the S.S. Noronic and S.S. Quebec?

Very substantial changes were made following the report by Mr. Justice Kellock in connection with the S.S. Noronic; in fact practically all the recommendations have been put into effect. The recommendations with regard to the S.S. Quebec have just been received and are being considered now.

River St. Lawrence ship channel service-

Many times the member for Assiniboia makes statements in the house concerning box cars and everything else-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member is very young.

Of course, he is very young, and he will learn in time. I have a few notes here to refresh my memory. When we are talking about pipe lines, let me say there is more to building a pipe line than most people realize. When a line of this type has to be constructed, the best engineers must be available. I would not have believed it myself-
Hear, hear.

It may be a joke to some, but you would never believe that if oil were running downhill through a steel pipe line for a distance of three miles, it would break that pipe. Therefore, in building these lines, it is necessary that previous experience should have a great deal to do with it. There must be certain blocks in these lines in order to keep back the pressure which is so great if these blocks are not in there. Another thing is this. It is quite a difficult job to curve these pipes to pass around the various rocks that are sometimes found in the way, and to go through the various coulees. All these bends must be of the same nature as the land. The parliamentary assistant, the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair), gets a big kick out of it. He is at least learning what I am trying to tell him, and I hope that it may be of some value in the future.

It is difficult for him to
learn.

With time, one can learn. I
have found that out myself. Pipe line construction today is a job of a different nature from what it used to be in years gone by. Had we had to build a line of this type, we will say twenty years ago, it would have been something beyond the stretch of imagination of any man. But with the modern machinery we have at the present time, I believe it is evident that mankind is getting to receive more and more the benefit of the scientific brains responsible for the construction of this machinery.
If one were to read this pamphlet put out by the Imperial Oil Company, he would find that it gave him an illustration of how the pipe is laid by modern machinery, how pipe is wrapped in order to keep rust away so that the line will therefore last a number of years. It is really magnificent to know how, during the past decade, modern science has at last found some method by means of which Canadians will have an opportunity to get the benefit of this development.

I have not much more to say about this line, except that I am sponsoring an allCanadian route before any part of a pipe line coming from Canada is built in the United States.

Will the hon. member

Surely.
Is grease ever used in wrapping a pipe line in order to avoid rust?

I am glad that the hon.
member has asked that question. Since he has asked me, I would say that the better the grease, the better the job. If my friend wants further information as to the better types of grease, I can give him that too.
I had a few notes here with regard to this line, and I think I have endeavoured to make some little contribution to this debate. If a large number of hon. members take part in this debate, and if they stick together, I think they can tell the board of transport commissioners in no uncertain terms-and that board is now overburdened and has had a terrible responsibility lately-in order to take the burden off their shoulders, that they will not allow any pipe line to be built outside of Canada before Canada's needs are first met.

Mr. Speaker, this house is a good crucible in which to work out national policies. I believe that it has great value for that purpose and, of course, for many others. But here we are able to discuss the pros and cons of various questions; and, generally speaking, a fairly satisfactory solution is worked out by the members of the house.
I believe most sincerely that the question raised by these bills which seek to grant charters for the building of pipe lines is one of the greatest importance to Canada at this time and is perhaps one of the most important ones we have had to solve for many years. As hon. members of the house will know, that great question is whether our natural resources are to be used first for the benefit of Canadians or whether they are to be shipped abroad in the unfinished state simply because, for the time being, that may seem to be the quickest way to make a little bit of money.
The question is so highly important now because of the place of iron, steel, oil and gas in the economy of any nation. No country in the modern world can become one of the leading nations without those particular resources. It so happens that in recent years Canada has found great deposits of iron ore, of oil and of natural gas. If properly used 80709-128
Border Pipeline Corporation these can help greatly to build this nation into a strong power. Therefore, although this subject has been discussed on numerous previous occasions in the house, I offer no apologies for going over the field again, because we have here before us this evening a bill submitted by a group of men whose purpose admittedly is to build a pipe line by means of which to bring oil from the fields in Alberta down into the states of Washington and Oregon, getting into those states by the shortest route.
It is the second chapter of the story which began two or three years ago. In 1949 a charter was granted to a company to pipe oil from Alberta to the east, the line going down to Superior, Wisconsin, rather than to Fort William and Port Arthur. As Your Honour knows, some of us protested that action. Incidentally, I believe the sponsor of that bill in this house is the same sponsor who is asking for this present charter.
Will the hon. member permit a question? Does he not agree that the bill to which he refers, which I sponsored a few years ago, has resulted in great benefits to Canada?

My answer to that question is this:	I believe that had that line been constructed to Fort William and Port Arthur it would have resulted in a great deal more benefit to Canada, not only at the present time but in the years ahead.
In one of the leading United States weeklies at that time-I refer to the V.S. News and World Report-there appeared an article entitled "Canada: oil's new hot spot." With the article there appeared a sketch of Canada showing the proposed pipe line east from Alberta right down into the United States at Superior and another west to the Pacific coast at Seattle, Tacoma and Portland. Tonight we are considering a bill for a group who propose to build the second leg of this particular plan, namely, an oil pipe line to the west coast of the United States.
The company will be known as "Border Pipeline Corporation." The line, as I have said, wall run from Alberta down across the southeastern corner of British Columbia, through the Crowsnest pass and then down into the city of Spokane in the state of Washington and to the city of Seattle where refineries are to be built. I presume it will also go to Tacoma, and a branch goes further south to the city of Portland in the state of Oregon. There is to be a branch to the north ending at or near the city of Vancouver. We have of course no way of making certain that this stub line up to Vancouver will ever be built. If this charter is granted and the company gets permission to go ahead, the

Border Pipeline Corporation final result may be that there will be refineries at Seattle and at Portland, while Vancouver and the rest of British Columbia may be getting their Canadian oil by tanker from the United States.
If the plan of this company is followed out the Vancouver area will be the only portion of British Columbia to get this crude oil by pipe line. There will be no chance to have refineries in any of the interior cities of our province, and at all times the oil which eventually may come to Vancouver will be subject to control by the federal authorities of the United States, and also by the state authorities of the state of Washington, because, as I have pointed out, the line would run through the United States before coming to the Canadian west coast. All this would take place although it is Canadian oil from the adjoining province of Alberta. Furthermore, J3ritish Columbians, being at the end of the line, will be paying the highest price for this Canadian oil.
Another very important feature is that if this oil pipe line is built through the United States it is practically certain that a natural gas pipe line will go by the same route. A year ago we thought that the gas line would be built first, but now there is a rush to get an oil pipe line to the Pacific coast, and it seems certain that the oil will be there ahead of the gas. Should this oil line go through the United States the result will be to make it cheaper to put a gas line by the same route, and we are very likely to find both our oil and our gas going through the United States, and we will only get what there is to run out at the end of the line.
I oppose this bill just as strongly as I possibly can, because I believe it should be a fundamental policy of this nation that Canadian resources must be made available to Canadians first. There could be no objection whatever to selling our surplus to the other nations, and in particular to our good friends of the United States; but they have built their nation on the very policy that I am advocating this evening, and they would be the last people to criticize us for doing the same thing as they have done since the founding of the republic.
Last year in the discussions on the natural gas bill we were met with the argument that there would be a monopoly; that it was not fair to have only one company incorporated. Incidentally, one very important point that I have omitted is that there will be only one oil pipe line to the coast, and only one gas pipe line. I think that is admitted by everyone interested in the question.

Border Pipeline Corporation asked for the building of this railway. There is a lot of information about the oil business that is not given to this house. I am no expert on oil, but I know that for thirty-five years we imported oil from the United States to Burrard inlet at Vancouver, and nobody seemed to be very bitter about that. If we had not got oil from the United States we would not have been able to run our automobiles or diesel engines in British Columbia. For thirty-five years our oil came either from California or from Peru. It was conveyed by tanker to ports on the west coast, and we were very glad to have it. British Columbia is one of the greatest markets for oil that there is.
Why send ours out then?

Therefore I say we should not speak of the Americans with bitterness, and I think it is time that we gave fair consideration to all these factors. I can give you a little personal information about something that happened to my advantage in connection with the oil business. When I went to British Columbia from Ontario I naturally saw the possibilities of that new country. I homesteaded crown land some twenty miles outside the city of Vancouver. There were stumps of course and rocks, and it was not very attractive. It was like some of the country we see in Glengarry or up in Pontiac county. The day came when the Imperial Oil Company of Canada, represented by Mr. Victor Ross, came to me and bought 60 acres of that land to form part of the site for the present loco refinery on Burrard inlet.

The oil business is a magic business. It is a great thing that we have these supplies in Alberta. Mr. Speaker, I rise to express my opposition to the bill, and I will give my reasons as I proceed. Before doing so, I want to draw the attention of the house to a rather interesting fact in connection with these bills that propose the piping of gas or oil from Canada through the United States, and in some cases back into Canada. It seems impossible for the companies concerned to get a sponsor from British Columbia. This bill is sponsored by an Ontario member. What is the reason for that? It is simply that all hon. members from

Border Pipeline Corporation British Columbia know that it is politically dangerous to sponsor a bill, whether it is for a gas or oil pipe line, that means the piping of gas or oil into the United States and thence to the coastal area without proceeding by an all-Canadian route.
I strongly oppose the bill now before us on two grounds. The first is the fact that the bill proposes to build a pipe line with private capital. We believe that pipe lines, railways and national efforts of this sort should certainly be under public ownership. That sentiment runs across party lines in this house. It is not only the C.C.F. who advocate the public ownership of pipe lines. Liberal members have expressed their support of public ownership.
Who?

Members of the Conservative party have expressed their support of public ownership. Of course the policy of the C.C.F. is to advocate public ownership of utilities such as these. In this house a year or so ago the leader of the coalition party from British Columbia rose and expressed his support for the public ownership of pipe lines.
Don't tag that name on me.

I refer to the brilliant member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson), with whom I do not always agree. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I appreciate the position taken by the minister and I shall look forward to hearing from him when he gets that reply from the Canadian National Railways. I am wondering, however, just what the minister meant when he referred to the legal aspect of the matter.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I just suggest one other thought. I do this because I presume that, when this matter gets studied by the minister and by the department, today's Hansard will probably be looked at. Therefore if one has a point to make, now is the time to make it. My suggestion is this. I suggest that when the minister or his officials are studying this matter, they look up the debate which took place in this house when the labour code was before us. As a matter of fact, if my memory serves me aright, that debate took place on June 17, 1948. I do not presume to remember every date on which anything takes place, but I have reason for remembering that date very well and the Minister of Transport will remember it too. An extremely important amendment to the labour code went through on that date, one I had fought for for many years. In the debate of that day the minister will find that the then minister of labour discussed the position of these people who, by the terms of the labour code, are excluded from automatic recognition and the automatic right to collective bargaining. The point was that although these people, including the people involved in management functions, are excluded from that automatic right, still there is no law against that right being accorded to them by any employer who wishes to do so. It is that view of the former minister of labour which I wish the Minister of Transport would look at when he is assessing the legal aspects.
That was the question that was in my mind: whether or not an amendment to the act would be necessary in order to do what my hon. friend requested.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is exactly the point. I am glad the minister raised it; because when, on June 17, 1948, an attempt was made to amend the act with respect to architects, I believe, that amendment was defeated. The minister of labour said then that even though that amendment was defeated, even though architects were excluded from the automatic right to collective bargaining, there was nothing to prevent them from having it wherever their employers were willing to accord it to them. That is what I am hoping the Canadian National Railways will be prepared to do with regard to these railway supervisors.

This afternoon when I mentioned this question of transportation of members of parliament, the minister did not give me any assurance that he was even

going to look into the matter. I am just wondering if he realizes the principle that is involved. It is customary for people to say that they do not care about the money, that it is the principle of the thing. I am not going to use quite that trite observation at this time; but to tell the truth, I cannot quite imagine the former member for Comox-Alberni, with his rather legalistic turn of mind, not making a protest when he got clipped year after year on this particular point. Probably he did. Even so, probably the same thing happened to him as happened to me. The hon. member for Danforth spoke in stentorian tones to the effect that probably more of us should pay our own way. But I can just imagine the squeals that he would make if, every week end when he went home-sometimes	perhaps on Thursday
night, probably more often late on Friday night-
No, not the hon. member for Danforth.

-if he had to pay some sum of money apart from what every other member of parliament pays. In those circumstances I am certain he would have supported the argument I made this afternoon. I am curious. This is an item for repair, operation and maintenance of official railway cars. Suppose the minister paid us a visit in British Columbia, and that he arrived at Vancouver. Suppose that someone suggested that the salmon was biting over in Campbell river and that he might like to take his car over there. Would he, as a matter of right, get transportation of his car to the island if he so requested? I am quite sure that he probably would not ask for it. But would he not have a right to do that?
The answer is no.

I am sorry to persist but is
the minister correct in that observation that the answer is no? Have you ever looked into it? Have you ever made a study of it?

I have not made a study
of it, but apparently the hon. gentleman is not conversant with the act. As I tried to explain to him this afternoon, the act does not provide free transportation for members of parliament by steamship companies. The act simply provides for transportation on railways, and it provides also for the making of regulations governing the issuance of transportation by the board of transport commissioners. The board of transport commissioners have no jurisdiction over the steamship companies. For that reason I gave the hon. gentleman the answer that I did this afternoon. When he now asks me if I am sure of my answer when I say no to him, may I say that the reason for saying no so quickly

arises out of the answer which I gave this afternoon. It is evident that I could not move a private car to the island without paying the cost of transportation on the steamship, unless the railway wanted to come forward and say, "Certainly take your car over; we will look after it."

Of course my point was that probably the act should be amended. Could it be amended?
I suppose it could.
Would you not think that, in equity to all members of parliament, it should be amended?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I should like to join my colleague on this matter mainly because some three or four years ago the two of us placed another issue on transportation before this house. As you will recall, it was the question of whether or not hon. members coming from their ridings to this house could travel by air under the statute in question. We had done some work on the matter and saw that in the House of Commons Act there was this provision for direct transportation. Those who live close to Ottawa felt that the train was good enough; but those coming from far out-of-the-way places felt that the intent of the people who framed the act was that we should have direct passage. I am extremely glad that in the end the Speaker, who was adjudicating on the matter, upheld our contention. I am perhaps in a little bit better position to raise the point which he originally made because in the Railway Act the clause to which he referred makes provision that members of parliament may travel as of right on the railways of Canada. I looked back in Hansard and found out that this was one of the few concessions that the railways gave in return for getting the many concessions that this country gave in the way of land rights, mineral rights and so on, to enable the construction of the railways to go ahead.
I think the intent was pretty clear, namely, that this was a concession to enable a member of parliament to come from his home to Ottawa as often as he wanted on the national railway systems, not the nationally owned system. And today that intent is certainly carried out, because those members

Supply-Transport
from Newfoundland can come from Newfoundland on the Canadian National railway and the Canadian National steamship services and arrive in Ottawa on their House of Commons passes. Those who come from New Brunswick find that they can travel through the United States, but they have to pay their fare when they travel through the United States on the Canadian railways, which is then a United States company, which is as separate from the Canadian railway company as is the Canadian Pacific Railway coast steamships. All you have to do is to send the receipts down to the Canadian Pacific Railway agent here and you get a refund. But there are three members of parliament here, the hon. member for Victoria, the Minister of Fisheries; the hon. member for Nanaimo, and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, who cannot get to parliament unless they pay the Canadian Pacific steamships their fare from Victoria to Vancouver or from Nanaimo to Vancouver. Why the Canadian Pacific Railway should refund the maritime members their fare and not make this concession to the three Vancouver island members I do not know.
This afternoon I raised the matter of subsidy which the Canadian Pacific steamships are not backward about asking for, a subsidy which is given them for their operation on the west coast. I can think of a little steamship line in my riding which does not get subsidies from the Department of Transport but it does extend the courtesy of a pass to the local members of parliament on their steamship lines because they feel that that was the sense of the original provision in the Railway Act.
I know that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni does not need the actual fare between Nanaimo and Vancouver. His predecessor who was also well endowed with this world's goods probably did not either; but it is more than that. It is the principle of the thing. There are three members of parliament who cannot come to parliament on their House of Commons passes, and I think quite frankly that the minister should pay a little attention to it, or perhaps hon. members should pay a little attention to it.
Nova Scotia members are in the same position.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Yes, therefore it rises above sectionalism. I think members of all parties should pay a little more attention to the subsidies we give to these Canadian steamships if the Canadian Pacific feels that it is necessary to adhere so closely to the letter of the law so far as the British Columbia members are concerned and yet be so

generous with their cash refunds so far as the New Brunswick members are concerned.

In case there may be a misapprehension so far as the members from Nova Scotia are concerned, those who use the Canadian Pacific steamship Princess Helene pay their fare on that ship and do not get a refund. The refund they get is when they go through the state of Maine by train.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I was just mentioning New Brunswick.
They do not travel by steamship.

I have just been informed that the Canadian Pacific inland steamships on Arrow lakes honour the passes. The hon. member for Kootenay West tells me that they give him the courtesy there and honour his pass. They do not give him a special pass. I have been told by certain Canadian Pacific Railway officials if I wish to make a submission in conjunction with the Minister of Fisheries-the Minister of Fisheries certainly must have a pass, I do not know. They suggested-
I would not think so.
Perhaps he does not have one. He should have one, certainly.
The Minister of Resources and Development does not have a pass on the Princess Helene.

He should have one on the Princess Helene. As I was saying, the hon. member for Kootenay West told me that his pass is honoured on the inland steamships of the Canadian Pacific Railway. When it comes to the point of going up the west coast of Vancouver island, $100,000 of a subsidy is paid. I am quite sure that if the hon. member for Nanaimo and I went to the Canadian Pacific steamships and said: Will you please give us a pass? We think probably you should. We did not oppose your subsidy in the house. Then they probably would. As a principle, I do not think that a member of parliament ought to barter his support or otherwise with any steamship or railway company of Canada. Once again, as a matter of principle, I think the minister owes it to us. The fact that we come from these far distances and live on islands should not be a disability to us, so far as members of parliament are concerned.
Owes what to you? I do not quite understand the hon. member.

The minister can get around his riding without paying any railway fare.

He can go by rail or by road. I have to travel literally hundreds of miles in my riding, and in some sections of it there are only steamship services. That is the only connection that is provided there. In order to get around and see my constituents I must pay. I have never minded that in the past. I think the principle is wrong. If a minister can go to his people by rail for nothing, then I should be able to travel on steamships, particularly on the ones that get very heavy subsidies from this house, for nothing. I should be able to go and visit my people in the same way.

I think probably some of us who have not this to contend with as members of parliament should rise and say something in support of the principle that is being asked for by the members of parliament who are involved. In fact, I think it might have been better if some of the rest of us who are not involved had known about this and had raised the issue, because I am quite sure that while an interpretation might have been placed upon something that was said by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, it would not make any difference to his attitude on subsidies, or public affairs generally.
What I was going to say was this: If those of us who have not to cross water are able to travel to the House of Commons without let or hindrance in this way, no matter how small the amount-probably it does not amount to a great deal to some members relatively, but the principle is there-
Certainly.

-I think some consideration might be given to the matter by the minister. I know that we cannot do anything here at the moment, but I think it is only proper that a few of us who are not personally involved in this matter should say that we think that the principle that the hon. gentleman is arguing for is a sound one and should be conceded.

What I was going to say when I rose a moment ago is this. The difficulty arises because of the fact that there is no body that has jurisdiction over these steamship operations, such as the one having jurisdiction over the railways. The board of transport commissioners provides the regulations governing the issuance of transportation. In this case I suppose it would be possible to meet the position with an amendment, but I certainly would not be prepared to bring down an amendment without more discussion on the matter. I think a question of that kind would have to be discussed with the

steamship companies involved. It is my feeling that if it were there would not be very much difficulty about it. Perhaps I can ask the maritime commission to give it some consideration.
While the maritime commission does not have jurisdiction over the operations of these steamship companies, yet it provides the subsidies that have already been mentioned, and I will ask the maritime commission to give it consideration to see if it is not possible, without an amendment of the Railway Act or of some act of parliament, to grant in these specific cases courtesy transportation.

I should think that what the minister has said would certainly agree with the views of the members. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
If the minister is going to take this matter up, there is one word I should like to say. I support the principle that has been raised, but it has been suggested in the discussion that one solution

Supply-Transport
to the problem might be for the Canadian Pacific Railway to make refunds to those who have to cross from Vancouver island to the mainland in the same way that it makes refunds to those who have to cross the state of Maine.
It seems to me what is needed is not a situation where certain hon. members get cash refunds from the Canadian Pacific Railway, but rather a law of this parliament providing that any necessary transportation is a matter of right. I am not suggesting that the law needs to be amended so that any hon. member of parliament can travel on any steamship at any time; but it does seem to me that the law could quite easily be	amended to provide
steamship transportation as of right where-ever that transportation is necessary to make a continuous trip from one part of Canada to another.
This is a matter which has interested me somewhat because of a story well known to many of us in Winnipeg. The first labour member ever to come to the parliament of Canada was Mr. Arthur Puttee, who was elected as the member for Winnipeg in 1900, fifty-one years ago. Mr. Puttee is today well on in years, but he is in good health and still lives in the city of Winnipeg.
At that time members of parliament for the most part made their trips to Ottawa by virtue of passes given to them by the various railways. The gifts of the railways in those days, so we are told, were quite generous in many cases, and hon. members felt they were under obligation to them. When Mr. Arthur Puttee was elected to come to Ottawa, though he was a workingman and it was not easy for him to find the money, he paid his own way, and sat up all the way. He was determined not to be under any obligation to the railway companies. It was not long before other hon. members felt the same way, and the law was amended so as to give transportation as of right, so that no hon. member was under any obligation to a railway company.
I think the situation that now obtains whereby the Canadian Pacific Railway makes refunds to those who cross the state of Maine should be changed, and that travel should be as of right. I would say the same should be the case for those who have to take a steamship at any place so as to make a continuous trip from one part of Canada to another.

That transportation could not by any stretch of the imagination be as of right, because it is in another country. This parliament has no authority to pass laws affecting other countries.

In so far as the first point raised by the hon. member, although I may be mistaken, I think perhaps the reason for the gratuitous transportation on railways is that parliament has always had jurisdiction over the railways, and provided the moneys voted originally for them. Not so, however, with the steamships, with the exception of steamships receiving subsidies. Many of the steamships which receive subsidies however would be of no use to hon. members. I believe that applies to the mail steamship operating between Vancouver and Victoria, which my hon. friend has in mind, and probably that is the one which would be used by the hon. member for Nanaimo. That perhaps is the reason why parliament, when it enacted legislation in the first instance, dealt with the railways alone, and not with steamships.
Do they not operate under charters granted by parliament?
Yes. Then, if one pursues it a step further, why not grant transportation on bus lines? After all, these are private corporations over which we certainly have no jurisdiction.
But we do not grant bus lines charters.

No, we do not; but sometimes bus lines are the property of railways. I was saying that bus lines often are operated by railways through subsidiary companies. I am just trying to be helpful in finding a reason why there has been a distinction as between railways and steamships.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: And as between members of parliament.
Well, unfortunately, that is the case. I do not think it will apply to many members of parliament.
About twenty of them.
As I have said, I am asking the maritime commission to give it their consideration.

Just so that the record may be complete, I think the hon. member for Yukon-Mackenzie River is perhaps under a greater disability than any other member in the house, in having to go from Skagway to Vancouver. I think that is particularly unfair and places an undue burden upon him.

When the minister is looking into this matter, perhaps he might look into the related matter of the status of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway. Passes with which members are furnished say that they are entitled to free transportation, with baggage, upon all railway trains in Canada. I

am informed however that does not entitle a member to free transportation upon the Pacific Great Eastern.
Let me make it clear at once that they have never placed the slightest difficulty in my way when travelling on that line on a passenger train., or using their freight facilities, in conformity with the regulations existing in that regard. However I understand that there is some peculiar local position affecting the Pacific Great Eastern to the end that that railway, not having been completed, it is not a railway within the definition of the point we are discussing.
Perhaps when the minister is making a general investigation of the matter he would look into this point, because there are certain portions of my riding I can reach only by using the Pacific Great Eastern.
I will do that.

Perhaps some word might be added from this corner of the house. I do not think I have been particularly backward at any time in past years in rising to support the rights of members of parliament. Predictions have been made at times that when I did so I would get it in the neck. I never have found that to be so.
It is my personal view that the same privileges granted to members of parliament on railways should be granted to them on steamships plying in Canadian waters between coastal ports. My reason for saying that is that it will be discovered in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms-and I am not raising a point of order-that a member of parliament represents not only his own constituency, but rather that he represents all the people in Canada.
I think that principle is behind the fact that there is written into the Railway Act the matter of transportation over any Canadian railway for members of parliament. How is one to get first-hand knowledge of the country if he cannot go everywhere? How can one get first-hand knowledge of those parts of the country served by steamships? I believe that all members of parliament should be given passes on all steamship lines plying Canadian waters, both inland, and coastal.
The railway trains and the steamships are being run anyway, whether a member is travelling on them or not. To take a member on board a railway or a steamship does not mean even an infinitesimal cost because the railroad or steamship do not supply berths and meals and therefore it is impossible for them to lose. I make these remarks because I believe we have a right as members of 80709-130
Supply-Transport
parliament representing the people of Canada to be able to travel anywhere we desire.

I understood the minister
was going to have this matter investigated by the commissioners, but I would say that it is not necessary to have any investigation with regard to the Borden-Tormentine car ferry, or any other car ferry, because our passes are good.
If it is subsidized and maintained at a loss by the Canadian government, everybody should travel free. If it is making money, then we cannot travel.
